transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-17
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Li (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Samantha Torres (NovaHealth Platform Lead), Elliot Chen (NovaHealth ML Eng), Raj Patel (NovaHealth CTO)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/pilot-notes (deck), https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/novapilot (benchmark spreadsheet)

Summary: quick sync on last week's caching changes; reviewed KV/prefix cache hit rates after canonicalization, looked at prompt reuse patterns, discussed TTL vs eviction, and next steps to run a production-like 48h benchmark with normalized prompts. Some security concerns around prefix caching and PII flagged; agreed to a follow-up compliance Q&A if pilot scales.

00:00 Marcus: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off — um — brief recap from last week, we rolled the prompt-normalization patch and increased the prefix canonicalization rules, priya and i will go through the numbers.
00:18 Priya: cool so quick TL;DR — baseline before patch, kv cache hit was around ~72% on our sample workload, prefix reuse about 54%. after normalization in the staging pilot we saw kv hit jump to ~86% and prefix reuse up to ~78% on the same trace. latency P50 improved from 220ms to 160ms for calls that hit cache.
00:42 Samantha: that's great, those numbers look promising. are those numbers from the full traffic or a sampled trace?
00:50 Priya: sampled trace — we ran a 6-hour extract with session-level grouping; full production traffic is noisier but we did some spot checks and the trend holds.
:01:05 Elliot: quick question — how are you measuring 'prefix reuse'? is that exact string matching or fuzzy? we have a lot of small paraphrases in our prompts.
01:16 Priya: good question — right now it's normalized-template matching; we canonicalize variable slots (dates, ids), strip non-deterministic tokens, lowercasing, and collapse whitespace. so not fuzzy embedding match, it's templated. that is why we saw a big uplift — many of your prompts were variations of the same template.
01:35 Marcus: also noted we bumped the KV cache TTL to 30m for the pilot; that helped hit rates for multi-step conversations. but for stateless single-turn calls we recommend a shorter TTL to avoid stale context.
01:50 Raj: couple of security things — prefix caching sounds like we might be storing partial user input. is that correct? what retention and encryption is in place?
02:02 Marcus: yes, good flag. prefix caching stores tokenized prefixes in volatile KV store, by default it's encrypted at rest in the pilot cluster and we don't persist long-term — TTLs apply. for Private deployments you can bring your KMS/HSM and control keys. we also support redaction rules so you can strip PII before caching.
02:24 Samantha: are redaction rules automatic or do we define patterns? some of our IDs are alphanumeric customer codes that look like random tokens.
02:33 Priya: currently pattern-based plus regex allow-list/deny-list; we can help build custome regex for NovaHealth. we also recommended a pre-processing layer to replace sensitive slots with stable tokens before caching.
02:48 Elliot: on the performance notes, any effect on throughput when we increased the normalization? like CPU overhead on the SE nodes?
02:55 Priya: negligible for our scale in pilot — normalization is a lightweight transformation done in the request path (~2-4ms) and most cost is in the model inference; the net win is lower model tokens per request because of cache hits.
03:12 Marcus: ok let's drill into the spreadsheet — priya, can you call out the timeline?
03:18 Priya: sure — table A is before, table B is after. interesting row: conversational session id 9b3c showed repeated prompt patterns, pre-change had 40% KV hits, post-change 92% — that case accounted for a big portion of tail latency reduction.
03:38 Elliot: nice. do you have the raw token counts per call for that session?
03:45 Priya: yep columns: input_tokens, output_tokens, kv_hit (true/false), prefix_match_id. i'll share the filtered extract.
03:55 Samantha: what's the recommended approach for canonicalization when prompts are free-text? we can't force strict templates on product teams overnight.
04:07 Priya: pragmatic approach — start with top-10 highest volume templates, canonicalize those server-side. for freer text, apply light normalization (lowercase, punctuation stripping) plus hash-based bucketing for low-volume cases so you still get some cache locality without over-collateralizing.
04:25 Marcus: also suggest a hybrid: deterministic templates for common flows (search, summarization), and an LSH/embedding-based approximate dedupe for long-tail natural language queries — but embedding-dedupe costs more CPU and complicates correctness.
04:40 Raj: embedding-dedupe — does that mean additional model calls for vectorization or is it inline?
04:47 Priya: vectorization is inline on the request path to produce a small embedding (we use a micro-encoder) or precompute at ingestion depending on your pipeline. again extra cost but useful if you have many paraphrases.
05:02 Elliot: we tried naive embedding dedupe earlier and saw some false positives — similar-but-different prompts collapsing — so we want conservative thresholds.
05:12 Priya: totally, threshold tuning is key; that's why we recommended pilot comparisons and A/Bing conservative vs aggressive dedupe.
05:20 Marcus: circling back to metrics — for this week's action we want a 48h run with canonical prompts; capture: KV hit rate, prefix reuse, P95 latency, tokens per request, and cost delta. please include a small sample of failing cases (where canonicalization broke).
05:37 Samantha: agreed. also legal flagged retention sentence — need explicit statement of where cached prefixes live and for how long. can you add that to the runbook?
05:46 Marcus: yes we'll add an appendix in the runbook with retention, encryption, redaction details.
05:53 Elliot: one more thing — what about model variant fallbacks? if cached prefix not available, do we route to a cheaper model first?
06:02 Priya: currently route policy is: try primary model variant, if capacity constrained or model overloaded we can route to cheaper quantized variant; cache is model-aware so hits depend on variant compatibility. we can add automatic fallback to a compatible variant if you want to prioritize cost.
06:20 Raj: for NovaHealth we care about quality, so prefer same-arch fallback only. cost fallback if latency SLOs degrade.
06:28 Marcus: noted. we'll wire routing policy to your preferences in the pilot config.
06:34 Samantha: any obvious tuning knobs we missed?
06:37 Priya: we covered TTL, canonicalization rules, dedupe threshold, model-aware cache keys, and retention/redaction. also recommend token-level caching (prefix kv) vs full prompt caching depending on your traffic pattern; token-level gives more reuse in long convo flows.
06:56 Elliot: about token-level kv, do you maintain KV per session or global namespace? we need per-tenant isolation.
07:05 Priya: per-tenant namespace by default for Dedicated/Private; in hosted pilot it's tenant-isolated logical namespaces with strict ACLs. we can push tighter isolation for NovaHealth if requested.
07:18 Samantha: ok good. next steps recap?
07:22 Marcus: so A) Marcus to share updated config and annotated changelog by Thursday (2026-03-19), B) Elliot to run 48h benchmark with canonical prompts and report stats by 2026-03-24, C) Priya to provide runbook snippet + canonicalization examples by 2026-03-19, D) Samantha to confirm any additional compliance/legal Qs by 2026-03-20, E) schedule follow-up compliance Q&A if needed week of 2026-03-31.
07:50 Raj: sounds good. can we also get a short note on expected cost delta if hit rate increases to 90%? just ballpark per million requests.
08:00 Marcus: yes we'll add an estimated cost table in the notes; ballpark numbers only.
08:08 Samantha: thanks everyone; we're seeing tangible wins. next sync same time next week?
08:13 Marcus: yes same time next week, i'll send invite. thanks all.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present in raw export — e.g., 'kv' sometimes 'kay vee' in text, 'canonical' sometimes 'cannonical', speaker labels from Fireflies occasionally map to 'Speaker 2' in raw export. Preserved informal phrasing and interruptions.

End of transcript.
